Ph.summary: A fixed multi-word expression, usually colloquial, learned as one unit.
Ph.description: Set phrases and sayings that are longer than a single word but are listed as one vocabulary item. Their meaning is often figurative, so they have to be memorized as a whole. Unlike 成語 (Id), they are usually colloquial and not restricted to four characters.

tests.text: Consists of several words, often a whole verb phrase or clause.
Meaning is usually not the sum of its parts.
Colloquial register, can be of any length.

examples.zh: 你這樣做是脫褲子放屁。
examples.en: Doing it like this is 'taking off your pants to fart' (completely unnecessary).

contrasts.note: 成語 are literary, classical in origin, and almost always four characters (一舉兩得). Ph are colloquial and of any length.

Id.summary: 成語: a literary idiom, nearly always four characters, often from classical texts.
Id.description: Four-character idioms (成語) are compact, literary expressions, many of which come from historical stories or classical Chinese. In a sentence they act like a single word, most often as a predicate or modifier.

tests.text: Almost always exactly four characters.
Literary or classical grammar inside (e.g. 而, 之, 以).
Cannot be split or changed; the whole idiom acts as one word.

examples.zh: 坐捷運又快又便宜，真是一舉兩得。
examples.en: Taking the MRT is fast and cheap, really killing two birds with one stone.

examples.zh: 到了國外就要入鄉隨俗。
examples.en: When you go abroad, you should do as the locals do.
He often gives up halfway through things.

contrasts.note: Ph are colloquial sayings of any length (脫褲子放屁); Id are four-character literary idioms.

Adv.summary: Goes before the verb to add degree, negation, frequency, scope or attitude; never directly before a noun.
Adv.description: Adverbs sit between the subject and the verb (or before another adverb) and modify the verb phrase. They cover degree (很, 太), negation (不, 沒), frequency (常), scope (也, 都), timing (就, 才) and the speaker's attitude (難道, 其實). Short one-syllable adverbs (才, 就, 還, 都, 又) are the hardest: on top of their basic meaning they carry the speaker's attitude. 都 is 'all' in 我們都去, but 'already' in 都十二點了.

tests.text: Position: Subject + Adv + Verb. Most adverbs cannot come before the subject.
Cannot modify a noun: *很人.
Cannot stand alone as an answer or form A-not-A questions: *也不也.
Order of several adverbs: 也 goes first (也都, 也常, 也不). Negation usually follows the adverb (比較不熱), but 常 follows 不 (不常), and with 都 the order changes the meaning: 都不 'none', 不都 'not all'.

examples.en: He often travels all over the place.
Don't tell me you don't know?
It's already twelve and you're still not asleep?

wrong.why: Adverbs go after the subject, right before the verb; they can't open the sentence.

examples.zh: 我都喜歡李老師、王老師。
examples.en: (meant: I like both Teacher Li and Teacher Wang)

wrong.why: 都 sums up what comes before it, so the things it covers must stand in front, here as a topic.
wrong.correct: 李老師、王老師，我都喜歡。

wrong.why: 快要…了 means 'soon, any moment now' and can't take a time word. With a time word use 就要…了.

examples.zh: 我們常常聊天、喝茶一起。
examples.en: (meant: we often chat and drink tea together)

wrong.why: Adverbs go before the verb, never at the end. You are together first, then you chat.
wrong.correct: 我們常常一起聊天、喝茶。

examples.en: (meant: foreign students are afraid of cockroaches)

wrong.why: 恐怕 is an adverb, 'I'm afraid that… / probably', not the verb 'to fear'. The sentence still needs a main verb.

contrasts.note: 也, 就 link clauses like conjunctions, but they must come after the subject (他也去). A conjunction like 而且 can start the clause (而且他也去).
Auxiliaries can answer alone and form A-not-A (會不會去？ 會。); adverbs can't (*常。).
Time words like 昨天 also go before the verb, but they are nouns: they can be the subject (昨天是星期一).

Conj.summary: Links words or clauses; often paired, like 雖然…但是 or 因為…所以.
Conj.description: Conjunctions join two nouns (和, 跟) or two clauses (而且, 雖然, 因為, 所以, 可是). Clause conjunctions frequently come in pairs, with an adverb like 也 or 就 in the second clause. 和, 跟 and 與 join only words (詞連); joining clauses (句連) takes other conjunctions or none at all. Using 跟 like English 'and' between clauses is a typical mistake.

tests.text: 和/跟 link nouns, and the two sides can be swapped: 我跟他 = 他跟我.
Clause conjunctions can stand before the subject: 因為他病了，所以…
Cannot be followed by aspect markers like 了.
和/跟/與 never join clauses: 'and' between clauses is usually left out.
Cause comes before effect, and 因為 and 所以 usually appear together, unlike English 'because' or 'so' alone.
要是 'if' can stand before or after the subject; the result clause takes the adverb 就 right before its predicate.

examples.en: He and I are both students.

examples.zh: 他會說中文，而且說得很好。
examples.en: He speaks Chinese, and he speaks it well.

examples.zh: 因為火車太慢了，所以我想坐高鐵。
examples.en: The train is too slow, so I want to take the high-speed rail.

examples.zh: 你要是沒空，我們就不要去逛夜市。
examples.en: If you don't have time, we won't go to the night market.

examples.zh: 他週末開車到紐約，跟我馬上打電話叫姊姊來一起吃飯。
examples.en: (meant: he drove to New York on the weekend, and I called my sister right away to come eat with us)

wrong.why: 跟 only joins nouns, it can't link two clauses like English 'and'. Leave it out, or use a clause connector like 然後.
wrong.correct: 他週末開車到紐約，我馬上打電話叫姊姊來一起吃飯。

contrasts.note: 跟 as Prep marks a companion before the verb (我常跟他吃飯 – an adverb can go before 跟). As Conj, 跟 joins two equal nouns (我跟他是同學).
也, 就, 才 also link clauses, but they are adverbs and must follow the subject.

Det.summary: Points to or picks out a noun: 這/那/哪/每/某 + (number) + measure word + noun.
Det.description: Determiners come first in a noun phrase and specify which or how many: demonstratives (這, 那), the question word 哪, and quantifiers like 每 and 某. They normally need a measure word before the noun.

tests.text: Pattern: Det + (Number) + M + N, e.g. 這三本書. The number 一 is often dropped: 哪一個 = 哪個.
Usually needs a measure word before the noun: 這本書.
每 + M + N almost always comes with 都 before the verb. 不 or 沒 goes after 都 (每天都不忙); 'not every' is 不是每…都.
這/那 can stand alone as a subject: 這是我的。
每 can take a number and measure word (每兩個人); the similar 各 can't (*各兩個人).

examples.en: One day I'll go to Taiwan.

examples.zh: 他朋友不是每天都去看電影。
examples.en: His friend doesn't go to the movies every day.

contrasts.note: Pronouns like 他 are nouns and can't take a measure word (*他個); 這 combines with one (這個).
The measure word comes after the determiner: 這(Det) 個(M) 人(N).

M.summary: Measure word (classifier) between a number/determiner and a noun; also units and counts of actions.
M.description: Chinese nouns cannot be counted directly: a measure word goes between the number or determiner and the noun. Measure words also include containers (碗, 杯), units (公尺, 公斤) and verbal measures that count how many times something happens (次, 頓, 遍). Which measure word a noun takes can't really be worked out by rule: 條 goes with 繩子, 河, 褲子, 法律 and 狗 alike, so learn the measure word together with each noun. Shape is a rough guide: 條 for long, flexible things (蛇, 魚), 根 for long, rigid things (棍子, 針), 枝 for long cylinders (筆, 蠟燭).

tests.text: Pattern: Number/Det + M + N, e.g. 兩張紙.
A number cannot directly precede a noun: *三書, 三本書. About 30 common measure words cover most needs at the start.
Verbal measures follow the verb: 去過三次.
'Two' before a measure word is 兩, not 二: 兩本書.

examples.en: I need two sheets of paper.
He ate three bowls of rice.

wrong.why: A number can't attach directly to a noun; a measure word must come between them.
Before a measure word 'two' is 兩. 二 is for counting and inside numbers (十二, 二十).

contrasts.note: 碗 is N in 一個碗 'a bowl' (it needs its own measure word), but M in 一碗飯 'a bowl of rice'.
Determiners come before the measure word (這個); a measure word never starts a noun phrase in standard usage.

N.summary: People, things, places and times; in this system also numbers, pronouns and 幾.
N.description: Nouns can be subjects and objects and can be counted with a measure word. Note that this classification counts numbers (五), pronouns (他, 我), time words (昨天) and the question word 幾 as nouns too.

tests.text: Can be subject or object: 學校很大 / 我去學校.
Can be preceded by Det + M: 這所學校.
Cannot be modified by 很 or negated by 不 directly: *很學校, *不學校.
Place words are built with a localizer (上, 裡, 前), which shortens step by step: 桌子的上面 → 桌子上面 → 桌子上 → 桌上.

After 在, a common noun needs a localizer to become a place (在房子裡面), while a place name takes none (在臺灣, *在臺灣裡面). The reference point comes first: 房子的前面 'in front of the house', 前面的房子 'the house in front'.
Time units go from larger to smaller (明天晚上, *晚上明天), and time comes before place: Time + Place + Event.

A subject is normally understood as someone known. A new, indefinite subject is introduced with 有: 有兩個學生來找你. 有 + thing + 在 + place says the same as place + 有 + thing, but the first is about the thing, the second about the place.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

wrong.why: Time words go before the verb or at the start of the sentence, never at the end as in English.

examples.source: Yuan et al. 2023, p. 16; ACCC 1, p. 139

wrong.why: 房子 is a thing, not a place. After 在 it needs a localizer such as 裡面 to name a location.

examples.en: There's a cellphone on the floor (talking about the floor: place + 有 + thing).
There's a cellphone on the floor (talking about the phone: 有 + thing + 在 + place).
(meant: the restaurant is next to the school)

wrong.why: 旁邊 'side' is always the side of something, and the whole comes before its part: 學校旁邊 'the school's side'.

contrasts.note: 昨天, 今天 go before the verb like adverbs, but can also be the subject (昨天很冷), so they are nouns.
Some words are both: 碗 is N in 一個碗, M in 一碗湯.
Adjective-like words (冷, 高) are state verbs, not nouns: they take 很 and work as predicates.

Prep.summary: Introduces a noun (place, target, source, companion) before the main verb: Prep + N + V.
Prep.description: Prepositions (also called coverbs) form a phrase with a noun that comes before the main verb, adding where, from where, toward whom, with whom or for whom the action happens. Many of them are also full verbs in other contexts. The order follows the order of events: you are at a place, or leave a starting point, before you act. This is why Prep phrases go before the verb, not after it as in English. 跟 alone has three roles: who you do something with (我跟我媽住), who you say something to (你跟他說了什麼) and who you get something from (你跟他要了多少錢).

tests.text: Pattern: Subject + Prep + N + Verb, e.g. 我在家吃飯.
Cannot be the only verb in the sentence.
Doesn't take 了, 過 or 著.
Only 在, 到 and 給 can also follow the verb, and then they mark where something ends up: 放在桌上, 寄給老師.
Negation goes before the preposition, not before the main verb: 他不在家吃飯, 我不跟他去.
In a 比 comparison the state verb takes no 很, 真 or 非常. How big the difference is goes after it: 貴一點, 貴得多.

examples.en: He is very good to me.
What did you say to him?
(meant: we have class in the classroom)

wrong.why: The place comes before the action: Prep + place goes before the verb.

examples.source: Yuan et al. 2023, p. 17, 29; ACCC 1, p. 119

examples.en: (meant: I just came back to the dorm from his place)

wrong.why: The starting point comes first, in the order things happen: 從 + place goes before the verb.

examples.source: Yuan et al. 2023, p. 28–29; ACCC 1, p. XII

examples.en: (meant: he won't microwave the baozi for me)

wrong.why: 不 negates the whole Prep + verb phrase, so it goes in front of the preposition.

examples.en: (meant: my phone is much more expensive than his)

wrong.why: 比 already says 'more'; the state verb after it can't take 很. Put the size of the difference after the verb.
wrong.correct: 我的手機比他的貴得多。

examples.en: (meant: he put his hand on the table)

wrong.why: 在 before the verb is where an activity takes place. Where something ends up after being moved goes after the verb: V在 + place.

contrasts.note: 在 and 給 are verbs when they are the only verb: 他在家 'he's at home', 他給我一本書 'he gave me a book'.
在 right before an action verb, with no place after it, marks an action in progress (李老師在上課). This 在 is listed as Vs, not Prep.
跟 is Prep when an adverb can go before it (我也跟他去); Conj when it joins two equal nouns (我跟他都是學生).
把 also brings an object before the verb, but this list classifies it as a particle.

Ptc.summary: Function words with purely grammatical meaning: 的, 得, 了, 嗎, 啊, 把, complements 完/掉, interjections.
Ptc.description: A broad category for words that carry grammar rather than content: structural particles (的, 得, 地), aspect markers (了, 過, 著), sentence-final mood particles (嗎, 吧, 呢, 啊), the 把 construction, resultative complements (完, 掉) and interjections (喂).

tests.text: Cannot be used on its own or answer a question.
Usually unstressed, often in the neutral tone.
Attaches to a word or the end of a sentence.
了 right after an action verb marks completion (我買了三張票); 了 at the end of a sentence marks a change (天冷了). The second is the easier one to learn.
Verbal 了 disappears in the negative: 我沒吃晚飯, never *沒吃了. The question form is V了…沒有?
的 between possessor and noun can be dropped only for close relations with a pronoun possessor: 我爸爸, but 李先生的爸爸.
With a 得 complement, negation goes inside the complement: 做得不好.
吧 at the end turns a command into a suggestion. A bare command (喝！) sounds blunt.
In Taiwan 著 is rarely progressive (他在吃飯, not 他吃著飯); it marks a lasting state (門開著) or a posture during another action (站著吃).
In 是…的, 是 can highlight who, when, where or how, but never the object: 我是昨天買的.
被 usually reports something unpleasant (錢包被偷了), so *他被升官了 sounds odd.
The object of 把 must be definite (這支手機, 他的書, or a bare noun meaning a known one): *把一支手機賣了. 沒 or 別 goes before 把.
V得 describes how something actually went (吃得很開心). It doesn't combine with 要, 會 or 應該, nor with a result complement (*學得學好了).
V著 can't take a duration: 想了一陣, not *想著一陣.
V1著V2 means doing V2 while in the state of V1 (坐著看球); two separate activities at once take 一邊…一邊….

examples.zh: 我去年每天都學了中文。
examples.en: (meant: last year I studied Chinese every day)

wrong.why: 了 marks a completed event, not past time. Habits and repeated actions take no 了, even in the past.
沒 says the event didn't happen, so there is nothing for 了 to mark as completed. Drop 了.
的 can be left out only after a pronoun (我爸爸). After a name or a noun it stays.
得 must follow a verb. When the verb has an object, repeat the verb before 得, or move the object to the front.

examples.source: Yuan et al. 2023, p. 118; ACCC 1, p. 92

examples.en: (meant: I want to sell the car)

wrong.why: A verb after 把 can't stand bare: it needs a result, a complement, or at least 了.

examples.en: (meant: I want to sell a phone)

wrong.why: 把 means doing something to a particular, known thing, so its object can't be indefinite (一支). Point to the phone, or drop 把.

examples.en: (meant: what was it that you bought?)

wrong.why: 是…的 can't focus the object. To focus the object, say 'what you bought is…': V的是 + object.

examples.zh: 我昨天半夜十二點才回家了。
examples.en: (meant: I didn't get home until midnight last night)

wrong.why: 才 'not until' already presents the event as late; it doesn't take 了.
wrong.correct: 我昨天半夜十二點才回家。

examples.zh: 我現在要甜食吃得越來越少了。
examples.en: (meant: I should eat less sweets now)

wrong.why: V得 describes how something actually turned out, so it can't follow 要 'should'. Say what you should do instead.

examples.zh: 和尚想著一陣，後來同意和他們住在一起。
examples.en: (meant: the monk thought for a while, then agreed to live with them)

wrong.why: 著 marks an ongoing state with no end point, so it can't take a duration. A completed stretch of time takes 了.
wrong.correct: 和尚想了一陣，後來同意和他們住在一起。

examples.zh: 商場不允許人走著吸菸。
examples.en: (meant: the mall doesn't allow smoking while walking)

wrong.why: V1著V2 makes V1 the manner of V2 (坐著吃). Two activities done at the same time take 一邊…一邊….
wrong.correct: 商場不允許人一邊走一邊吸菸。

examples.zh: 小明沒給老師把作業交。
examples.en: (meant: Xiaoming didn't hand his homework in to the teacher)

wrong.why: The 把 phrase goes right before its verb, and the receiver follows the verb with 給: 把 + thing + V給 + person.
wrong.correct: 小明沒把作業交給老師。

examples.zh: 他把錢拿了從錢包出來。
examples.en: (meant: he took the money out of his wallet)

wrong.why: 從 + place goes before the verb, and the direction (出來) attaches straight to the verb, with 了 at the end.
wrong.correct: 他把錢從錢包拿出來了。

contrasts.note: 了 marks completion as a particle after the verb; 已經 'already' is an adverb before the verb.
完 is a particle as a complement (吃完), but a process verb on its own (電影完了).
把 behaves like a preposition but is listed as Ptc.

V.summary: Transitive action verb: something you do to an object; can be in progress (在) but takes no 很.
V.description: Action verbs describe deliberate activities. V marks the ones that take a direct object. They can be in progress (在), completed (了), experienced (過) and given as commands. V著 usually sets the background for another verb (騎著腳踏車去學校); on its own (他騎著腳踏車) it sounds unfinished. Teng also sorts action verbs by direction: 'outward' verbs send the object away from the subject (賣 'sell', 告訴 'tell'), 'inward' verbs bring it in (買 'buy', 問 'ask'). This matters for 把 and for double objects.

tests.text: Takes a direct object: 買東西, 做飯.
Can be progressive: 他在做飯.
Can't take degree adverbs: *很買.
Negation: 不 = won't / doesn't, 沒 = didn't.
Can be a command: 快說！ 別買！
With 把 when there is a result: 把飯吃完了.
把 + bare verb + 了 works only with outward verbs: 我把房子賣了. Inward verbs need a complement: 我把房子買下來了.
A duration follows the verb. With an object, repeat the verb (教中文教一年) or move the object to the front (房子他只租了半年).
Doubling means 'a little': 看看, and only the verb doubles, not the object: 做做飯. VV看 'try and see' takes no object after it: *喝喝看咖啡.
Double objects depend on the verb: 賣他一張卡 works, *買他一張卡 and *寄他一張卡 don't. V + thing + 給 + person works for all: 寄一張卡給他.
To say what is somewhere, a transitive verb drops its doer: place + V著 + thing, 牆上掛著一張畫.

examples.en: I want to buy a coat.
He rides his bike to school.
He rented the place for half a year.

wrong.why: Action verbs can't be modified by 很; only state verbs can. Use a frequency adverb instead.
買 is an 'inward' verb: the house comes to you. 把 + bare verb + 了 only works with 'outward' verbs like 賣; inward verbs need a complement.

examples.en: (meant: I sent him a Christmas card)

wrong.why: 寄 can't take two objects directly. Put the person after 給, either after the thing or before the verb.

examples.zh: 在牆上，我還掛著幾張全家的照片。
examples.en: (meant: there are also a few family photos hanging on the wall)

wrong.why: To say what is somewhere, start with the place (without 在) and leave out who put it there: place + V著 + thing.
wrong.correct: 牆上還掛著幾張全家的照片。

contrasts.note: 喜歡 also takes an object but describes a state: it takes 很 (很喜歡) and no 在.
忘記 takes an object but is an instant change: no 在 (*在忘記), negated with 沒.
Vi are action verbs without a direct object.

Vi.summary: Intransitive action verb: an activity with no direct object (跑, 坐, 睡, 笑).
Vi.description: Action verbs that don't take a direct object. Any target or location is introduced by a preposition before the verb instead (在椅子上坐, 對我笑). Otherwise they behave like V.

tests.text: Complete without an object: 孩子在笑.
Location/target goes in a preposition phrase: 跟朋友跑.
Can be progressive (在), take 了/過, be a command (請坐).
No degree adverbs: *很跑.
Shows what is somewhere: place + V著 + new noun, 台上站著一個人.

examples.zh: 他每天早上跑半個小時。
examples.en: He runs for half an hour every morning.
A student is sitting in the classroom.
(meant: I sat in the corner the whole time)

wrong.why: In V在+place the 在 phrase marks where you end up, so the verb can't take 著. Use either 坐在角落 or 在角落坐著.

contrasts.note: 買 sounds incomplete without an object (他在買…什麼？); 跑 doesn't.
跑 is Vi; 跑步 (run + step) is V-sep: 跑了一個小時的步.
Vs describe states and take 很 (很累); Vi describe activities and take 在 (在跑).

V-sep.summary: Separable action verb: a verb+object compound that can be split (唱了一首歌).
V-sep.description: 離合詞 are verb-object compounds that act as one verb but can be split: aspect markers, durations, measures and modifiers go between the verb and its built-in object. Because they already contain an object, they can't take another one. Not every compound allows every split, so learn the common pattern of each one. When the noun half is generic, 了 usually follows the whole compound: 你吃飯了嗎 'have you eaten?', while 你吃了飯嗎 sounds like asking about the rice. Teng points out that many of these are a verb with a generic object that together name one activity (教書 'teach', 唱歌 'sing'): the object refers to nothing specific, so you can't ask about it. From 他是教書的 you can't ask *他教哪一本書.

tests.text: Things go in the middle: 唱了兩首歌, 上了一個小時的網, 打過架.
tests.source: Yuan et al. 2023, p. 75; ACCC 1, p. 190, 339

tests.text: No second object: *見面他, use 跟他見面.
Reduplicates as AAB: 唱唱歌, 上上網 (not *唱歌唱歌).
Behaves like an action verb otherwise: 在唱歌, no 很.
了 test: if 了 fits in the middle (跳了舞), other material usually can too. But each compound has its own patterns: 見了他一面, not *見了他的面.
了 alone in the middle sounds unfinished when the object is generic (*他教了書, *他留了學); add a duration or amount (教了三年書) or put 了 at the end.
tests.source: Teng 2009, p. 109; Yuan et al. 2023, p. 74

tests.text: Some splits are allowed but sound incomplete on their own: ?我今天跑了步 needs more (跑了兩個小時的步) or 了 after the whole verb (跑步了).

examples.zh: 我們每天上八個鐘頭的班。
examples.en: We work eight hours a day.

wrong.why: 見面 already contains its own object (面), so it can't take another one; the other person is introduced with 跟.
Each separable verb splits in its own way. 見面 doesn't take a possessive inside; the person goes after 了 with 一面, or before the verb with 跟.

contrasts.note: 生氣 also splits (生他的氣) but is a state: it takes 很 (很生氣). Action ones don't (*很唱歌).
結婚 also splits (結了婚) but is a one-time change: negated with 沒 and not progressive.
Plain Vi like 跑 can't be split; 跑步 can.

Vs.summary: State verb ≈ English adjective: a quality that takes 很 and is a predicate without 是.
Vs.description: Most English adjectives are state verbs in Chinese. They work as the predicate directly (no 是), take degree adverbs, and can also modify nouns (with or without 的). With 了 they express a change of state (天冷了).

tests.text: Takes degree adverbs: 很冷, 太貴, 非常漂亮.
Predicate without 是: 他很高 (*他是高).
A plain statement needs 很, 不 or another adverb before the Vs. This 很 is unstressed; stressed, it means 'very'.
Negated with 不: 不冷.
Not progressive: *在冷.
Can modify a noun: 高樓, 漂亮的衣服.
有一點 + Vs is a mild complaint, so it only takes unwelcome qualities: 有一點貴, *有一點漂亮.
早, 晚, 快, 慢, 多, 少 can go before the verb for what is planned (明天早一點來) or after it for how it turned out (我來早了).
好/難 + a perception verb make one word (好吃, 難看); with an action verb they mean 'easy/hard to' (好學, 難找).
很有/很沒 + noun chunks act as Vs: 很有名, 很有道理, 很沒禮貌.

examples.en: What you say makes a lot of sense.

wrong.why: State verbs are predicates on their own and don't take 是; 很 is the neutral link instead.

examples.en: (meant: his younger sister is quite pretty)

wrong.why: 有一點 marks something as a bit too much, a complaint, so it doesn't go with a compliment.

contrasts.note: 壞 is Vs 'bad' in 他很壞, but Vp 'broken' in 電腦壞了: process verbs take no 很 and are negated with 沒.
新 works both ways (新書 / 書很新); 公共 only before a noun (公共汽車, *很公共).
高 can modify a noun directly (高樓); 多 can't (*多人, use 很多人).
Vs have no object (*很高他); Vst do (很喜歡他).

Vst.summary: Transitive state verb: a feeling, attitude or knowledge about an object; takes 很 (很喜歡他).
Vst.description: State verbs that take an object, mostly about emotions, attitudes and cognition. Like Vs they take degree adverbs and 不, and are not progressive; unlike Vs they take an object.

tests.text: Takes an object: 喜歡音樂, 關心你.
Takes degree adverbs (most of them): 很喜歡, 非常同意.
Negated with 不: 不同意.
Not progressive: *在喜歡.
Not used with 把: *我把他喜歡.
有 is an exception among state verbs: it is negated only with 沒, never 不: 我沒有書, *我不有書.
Even with Vst, 很 doesn't fit every use: 他很有錢 but not *他很有兩億元; 他很知道做人 ('knows how to treat people') but not *他很知道我的電話號碼.

examples.en: Parents all care about their children.
I don't agree with your view.

wrong.why: 把 needs an action verb that does something to the object, with a result. A state verb like 喜歡 can't be used with it.

examples.en: (meant: as a child I liked ants)

wrong.why: 了 isn't a past tense. A liking that lasted through a period in the past is a state and takes no 了.

contrasts.note: 買 is an action: 在買 works, *很買 doesn't. 喜歡 is the reverse.
會 is Vst when followed by a noun (他會中文), Vaux when followed by a verb (他會說中文).
Vs don't take an object: 他很高, but 他很喜歡你.

Vs-attr.summary: State verb used only before a noun; it can't be the predicate or take 很 (公共汽車, *很公共).
Vs-attr.description: Non-gradable classifying words (區別詞, 'non-predicate adjectives'). They sort nouns into kinds: wild vs. domestic, public vs. private. They only appear directly before a noun, sometimes with 的, and can't be the predicate of a sentence.

tests.text: Only before a noun: 野生動物, 公共廁所.
Not a predicate: *這個廁所很公共, *這條路很主要.
No degree adverbs: *很野生.
As a predicate it needs 是…的: 這些動物是野生的.

examples.en: There are many wild animals here.
I take the bus to work.

wrong.why: Attributive-only state verbs can only stand before a noun; they can't be the predicate or take 很.

contrasts.note: Regular Vs work both before nouns and as predicates (新書 / 這本書很新).
The opposite restriction: Vs-pred are only predicates, Vs-attr only modifiers.

Vs-pred.summary: State verb used only as a predicate; it can't directly modify a noun (人很多, *多人).
Vs-pred.description: State verbs that can be the predicate of a sentence but can't be placed directly before a noun. To modify a noun they need a helper, e.g. 很多人 instead of *多人.

tests.text: Works as a predicate: 錢不夠, 人很多.
Not directly before a noun: *多人, *少錢, *夠時間.
Takes degree adverbs and 不 like other Vs.
多 and 少 can go right before a verb, meaning 'more/less than planned': 多穿衣服, 少看電視.

examples.en: There are a lot of people here.

examples.zh: 我中文不好，應該多看書，少看電視。
examples.en: My Chinese isn't good; I should read more and watch less TV.

wrong.why: Predicative-only state verbs can't directly modify a noun; 多 needs 很 in front to do so.
English 'enough' can stand before a noun, but 夠 can only be the predicate: say that the money isn't enough.

contrasts.note: Regular Vs can modify nouns directly (高樓, 冷水); Vs-pred need 很 (很多人).
The opposite restriction: Vs-attr only before nouns, never predicates.

Vs-sep.summary: Separable state verb: a verb+object compound describing a feeling or state; takes 很 and can split (生他的氣).
Vs-sep.description: 離合詞 that describe states or emotions. They take degree adverbs like other state verbs, and like other separable verbs, the 'object' half can be split off to insert a person or modifier.

tests.text: Takes degree adverbs: 很生氣, 很放心.
Splits to include a person: 生他的氣 (*生氣他).
Negated with 不: 不放心.
Not every word listed as separable really splits: 幽默 (a loan of 'humor') is never split.

wrong.why: 生氣 already contains its own object (氣), so the person goes inside the split verb: 生 X 的氣.

contrasts.note: Action compounds don't take 很 (*很唱歌); state compounds do (很生氣).
Plain Vs (冷, 高) don't split.
Process compounds like 生病 are one-time changes: *很生病, 沒生病.
擔心 is often taught as separable (擔什麼心), but in speech it's mostly used like Vst with a direct object: 我很擔心他.

Vaux.summary: Auxiliary (modal) verb before another verb: ability, permission, possibility, obligation (會, 可以, 應該).
Vaux.description: Modal verbs that come before a main verb and add ability (會, 能), permission (可以), obligation (應該, 得), desire or intention (要, 想) and possibility. Like verbs, they can be negated, form A-not-A questions and serve as short answers. English 'can' splits into three: 會 (a learned skill), 能 (able, possible) and 可以 (allowed). One English word mapping to several Chinese ones is the hardest kind of difference for learners.

tests.text: Followed by a verb phrase: 會說, 可以去.
A-not-A question: 會不會？ 可不可以？ The auxiliary, not the main verb, is doubled: 能不能照相.
Can answer alone: 會。/ 不可以。
No 了, 過, 著: *會了說.
會 has two meanings: a learned skill (他會做飯) and likelihood (我明天會去看他).
不可以 only forbids (你不可以在這裡照相); the question 可不可以 can ask about either permission or possibility.

examples.en: You should sleep a bit earlier.

examples.zh: 他明天不會去上書法課。
examples.en: He won't go to calligraphy class tomorrow.

contrasts.note: 會 + noun is Vst (我會中文); 想 + noun is 'miss' (我很想你).
要 + noun is a verb 'want' (我要咖啡); 要 + verb is Vaux (我要去).
Adverbs also precede the verb but can't answer alone or form A-not-A (*也不也).

Vp.summary: Intransitive process verb: an instant change of state (破, 死, 感冒); negated with 沒, no 很, no 在.
Vp.description: Process verbs describe the moment something changes from one state to another, with the result being what matters. They almost always appear with 了, and since the change is instant, they can't be in progress.

tests.text: Usually with 了: 杯子破了.
Negated with 沒: 沒壞, not *不壞 (as 'not broken').
No degree adverbs: *很死.
Not progressive: *在死.
The noun after a Vp is its subject, not an object: in 王冕七歲死了父親 it is the father who died. This order reports something appearing or disappearing: 昨天大火死了不少人.
tests.source: Teng 2009, p. 105; Yuan et al. 2023, p. 22; ACCC 1, p. XIII–XIV

examples.en: Quite a few people died in this typhoon.

examples.zh: 我還沒決定要不要去旅行。
examples.en: I haven't decided yet whether to travel.

examples.zh: 那棵樹最近掉了不少葉子。
examples.en: That tree has lost a lot of leaves lately.

wrong.why: 破 is intransitive: the cup breaks, nobody 破s it. To say who broke it, use an action verb with 破 as its result: 打破.
病 'get sick' is a change, not a quality, so it can't take 很. Use 了 for the change, or 病得很重 for how bad it is.

contrasts.note: 壞: 他很壞 'he's bad' is Vs; 電腦壞了 'the computer broke' is Vp. 很 and 不 point to Vs, 了 and 沒 to Vp. Likewise 死 is Vp in 他死了, but Vs in 他的腦筋很死 'he's stubborn'.
Vpt are also instant changes but take an object (忘記他的名字).
Vi are activities that last (在跑); Vp are instant changes (*在破).

Vpt.summary: Transitive process verb: an instant change involving an object (忘記, 變成, 丟); negated with 沒.
Vpt.description: Process verbs that take an object. The event is a change that happens at a point in time (forgetting, becoming, losing) rather than an activity that lasts. 變成 + noun names the result (變成冰); 變得 + state verb describes the new state (變得很冷).

tests.text: Takes an object: 忘記他的名字, 變成冰.
Negated with 沒: 我沒忘記.
No degree adverbs: *很忘記.
Not progressive: *在忘記.
變得 + description reports a change that has happened (他最近變得胖了些); it sounds wrong in a hypothetical or with 會: *我會變得很興奮回家.

contrasts.note: Action verbs can be in progress (在買); process verbs can't (*在忘記). 丟 'throw away' is an action (在丟垃圾), 丟 'lose' is Vpt.
記得 'remember' is a state (很記得, 不記得); 忘記 'forget' is a change (沒忘記).
Vp take no object (杯子破了).

Vp-sep.summary: Separable process verb: a verb+object compound for a one-time change (結婚, 畢業); splits as 結了婚.
Vp-sep.description: 離合詞 that describe a change of state: getting married, getting sick, graduating. They split like other separable verbs and are negated with 沒 like other process verbs. The person or place involved goes in a preposition phrase.

tests.text: Splits: 結了婚, 結過兩次婚, 生了一場病, 畢了業.
No direct object: *結婚她, use 跟她結婚; *畢業大學, use 從大學畢業.
Negated with 沒: 還沒結婚.
No 很, not progressive: *很結婚.
Time since the change goes after the whole verb: 畢業三年了, 結婚十年了.

examples.zh: 我上個月生了一場大病。
examples.en: I was seriously ill last month.
She graduates from university next year.

wrong.why: 結婚 already contains its own object (婚), so it can't take another one; the partner is introduced with 跟.
Not every separable verb accepts a duration inside. Time since a one-time change goes after the whole verb.

contrasts.note: Action compounds can be in progress (在唱歌); process compounds can't.
生氣 is a state (很生氣); 生病 is a change (*很生病, 他生病了).
Plain Vp (破, 死) don't split.
